strengths: Timely and clinically motivated problem: interpretable, evidence-grounded medical deepfake detection with a 'localize-then-analyze' (pre-hoc) formulation that is a meaningful alternative to post-hoc rationalization.

Substantial resource contribution: MedForge-90K (90K images, 3 modalities, 19 pathologies, 10 editing models) with a well-documented writer–editor–diagnoser construction pipeline, expert-formulated detection guidelines, and detailed annotation protocols in the appendix.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation: in-domain, cross-model, and cross-forgery OOD settings, multiple specialized and generic baselines, ablations over response components, reward terms, and backbones (Table 3).

The core ablation (Part A) is honest and informative: removing bbox grounding barely changes accuracy but collapses Judge Score (53.9), nicely demonstrating that grounding supervision, not accuracy, is what the framework adds.
Good reproducibility surface: released code/data (footnote 1), full prompts, hyperparameters, reward weights, and judge prompts are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Circularity concerns in supervision and evaluation: rationales are generated by Gemini guided by pixel-difference-derived boxes, and 'reasoning quality' is then scored by MLLM-as-judge against these same LLM-generated ground truths. There is no human/expert evaluation of rationale quality, so 'expert-aligned' claims are only as strong as the unverified LLM annotations; the claimed 16.2% hallucination reduction rests on 100 samples judged by LLMs with known self-preference bias (e.g., Gemini 3 Pro judging its own outputs in Table 2).

Benchmark saturation and potential leakage: the test set is generated by the same pipeline (same writers, editors, verification loop) as training data, and gold forgery locations are derived by pixel-differencing the forged image against its source—making localization ground truth trivially recoverable from construction rather than clinically labeled. Near-perfect accuracy (99.2%+) suggests the task may be largely solved by pipeline artifacts (e.g., resampling to 1024×1024) rather than by genuine forgery reasoning; generalization to independently produced medical forgeries is untested.

Marginal or inconsistent evidence for some headline claims: the 7.65% accuracy gain comes with the proposed model scoring below Gemini 3 Pro under the Gemini judge (73.9 vs 76.2), which the text soft-pedals; ablation deltas are tiny (IoU differences of 0.01–0.02 used to argue R_bbox is 'essential'; accuracy gains of 0.1% for R_form), and Table 3 contains errors (e.g., '79,1').

Methodological novelty is limited: the contribution is essentially SFT + standard GSPO with new reward terms; the reward design (format/classification/coverage rewards) is a fairly conventional RLVR recipe. The framing as 'Forgery-aware GSPO' oversells an incremental combination.

Writing and presentation issues: multiple typos ('Nanao-Banana', 'Forgrey', 'Reaosning', 'aronud', 'Mortality-specific'), a duplicated 'Formatting Reward' bullet in Appendix B.4, and inconsistent claims (Limitations section says 'two main limitations' then lists three). These reduce polish and raise doubts about carefulness.

Evaluation asymmetry: specialized baselines are retrained on MedForge-90K under possibly mismatched configurations (336×336 inputs for SIDA vs 1024×1024 for the proposed model), so part of the large margin over baselines may reflect resolution/access advantages rather than the method.

strengths: Medically grounded deepfake detection is a timely and socially relevant problem, and the 'localize-then-analyze' (pre-hoc grounding) framing is a reasonable and well-motivated design principle for trustworthy explanations.

MedForge-90K is a substantial resource: ~90K samples across three modalities, 19 pathologies, and 10 editing models, with bounding-box-level edit localization and structured reasoning annotations. If released as described, it would address a real data gap relative to prior medical deepfake benchmarks.

The paper is generally well organized: the task formulation (Sec. 4.1), the two-stage SFT + GSPO pipeline, the reward decomposition (grounding coverage, format, classification), and the ablation structure are clearly described.

The ablation in Table 3 (Part A) makes a genuinely useful point: a model can achieve near-ceiling binary accuracy while its explanations collapse without spatial supervision (Judge Score 53.9 vs 90.2), which supports the paper's central argument that grounding must be an explicit objective rather than an afterthought.
OOD evaluation settings (Cross-Model, Cross-Forgery) are an appropriate attempt to test generalization beyond in-domain detection.
weaknesses: Circular evaluation undermines the central validity claims. The reasoning annotations are generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro; the primary judge is Gemini 3 Pro / Qwen3-VL-Plus; and the proposed model is Qwen3-VL-8B-based. Judges appear to share training lineage and stylistic conventions with both the annotation pipeline and the proposed system (Gemini 3 Pro is simultaneously a baseline and a judge; Qwen3-VL-Plus is both a baseline and a judge). This creates self-preference bias that plausibly inflates the 'MLLM-as-Judge' results, which are the paper's key evidence for 'trustworthy, expert-aligned explanations'.

The claimed 'human expert-guided' annotation is not substantiated. No information is given on the number, qualifications, or actual role of the medical experts; the pipeline as described is MLLM-driven (Gemini 2.5/3 Pro as writer/diagnoser/annotator) with guidelines injected into prompts. There is no human verification study of annotation quality, no inter-annotator agreement, and no clinician evaluation of the generated explanations — despite repeated claims of 'clinically rigorous' and 'expert-aligned' output.

Near-ceiling results (99%+ accuracy in-domain, 93-96% OOD, margins of 25-30 points over baselines trained on the same data) are suspicious and suggest the benchmark may be artificially easy, e.g., due to systematic artifacts of the generation pipeline (CVA-derived masks from Nano-Banana used as inpainting inputs, Gemini-loop filtering creating homogeneous edit styles). No analysis is provided to rule out shortcut features, and no human-detection or cross-dataset (real-world forgery) validation is reported.

MLLM-as-Judge protocol is weakly designed: only 100 samples, single-run scores with no variance or significance testing, judges given ground-truth explanations to compare against (measuring similarity to Gemini-generated rationales rather than factual correctness against the image), and the 'Visual Hallucination' metric direction/behavior across tables is confusing (generic MLLMs outscore specialized detectors, which contradicts the paper's own narrative).

Reproducibility is compromised. The code/data release footnote is incomplete (no URL), and the pipeline depends on closed APIs (Gemini 2.5/3 Pro, Nano-Banana, GPT-Image, Seedream) whose outputs cannot be regenerated. Combined with single-run evaluation and no released judge prompts/scripts beyond a static prompt box, independent verification is difficult.

The technical novelty of the method is limited. Localize-then-explain MLLM detectors exist (SIDA, FakeShield, Veritas, FakeReasoning); the main deltas are the medical domain adaptation and a straightforward reward reshaping (coverage-based sigmoid, format/classification rewards) applied to off-the-shelf GSPO. Ablations show the GSPO gains are marginal in accuracy (99.13 vs 99.23) and small on judge scores (~2.5 points), so the headline claims of '7.65% accuracy improvement and 16.2% hallucination reduction' largely reflect benchmark design rather than a strong methodological advance.

Experimental design details raise further concerns: 'Cross-Model' excludes four generators from training but the relationship to the default test set is ambiguously described; the 5:1:3 split rationale is unexplained; several baselines use much weaker backbones (LLaVA-1.5 at 336x336) than the proposed Qwen3-VL-8B, confounding model-capacity comparisons; qualitative Figure 4 examples appear cherry-picked.

Presentation defects: numerous typos in figures/tables ('Forgrey', 'Reaosning', 'aronud', '79,1', 'Gemini-2.5-Flash-Image' naming inconsistencies, duplicated 'Formatting Reward' bullet in B.4 with contradictory descriptions), Table 2 judge/baseline identity confusion, and inconsistent metric framing between the main text and Appendix B.3.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and socially important problem: medical image forgery detection with clinically verifiable, interpretable evidence, and clearly motivates why existing black-box detectors and post-hoc MLLM explainers are insufficient.

MedForge-90K is a substantial resource: ~90K images across three modalities, 19 pathologies, 10 state-of-the-art editing models, with localization masks and structured reasoning annotations. The construction pipeline (writer-editor-diagnoser loop, CVA-derived ground-truth boxes, hierarchical expert guidelines) is described in unusual detail in the appendix, including full prompt templates.
The core idea of localize-then-analyze (forcing bbox prediction before reasoning) is well-motivated and is operationalized concretely in the task formulation and the shaping of the grounding reward.

The experimental protocol covers in-domain, cross-model, and cross-forgery OOD settings, and the ablation study (Table 3) is genuinely informative: it isolates the reasoning components and shows the expected trade-off (binary classification gives the best raw accuracy, but the judge score collapses without bbox grounding), which supports the paper's central argument about grounding.
Reproducibility support is relatively strong: hyperparameters, training configurations for baselines, judge prompts, and reward implementations are all provided, and code/data release is promised.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity is a significant concern. Ground-truth rationales are generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro, and the primary reasoning-quality metric is MLLM-as-judge using Gemini 3 Pro / Qwen3-VL-Plus against those same annotations. A model trained on Gemini-generated rationales and judged by a similar model against those rationales is likely to be favored; independent human evaluation (even on a small subset, with stated expert credentials and agreement statistics) is missing. The 'human expert-guided annotation' involvement is never quantified (number of experts, validation protocol, inter-annotator agreement).

Benchmark realism and difficulty are questionable. Ground-truth boxes come from pixel-wise |Iforged − Ireal| differences, which are trivially available for synthetic edits; in-domain accuracy of 99.2% (vs. 68.3% for Gemini 3 Pro) suggests either a highly learnable shortcut or possible leakage, and raises doubt about whether the benchmark measures clinically meaningful forensic skill. No statistical significance, seeds, or variance are reported anywhere.

Claim-evidence mismatches. The abstract claims GSPO 'reduces hallucinations by 16.2%', but the 16.2% figure is the comparison to AIGC-Holmes in Table 2; the actual gain from GSPO over the no-GSPO variant is only +2.5 average judge points (and LC/VH improvements under the Gemini judge are near-zero or negative, e.g., 71.6→71.1 LC). The abstract framing overstates the marginal contribution of the proposed optimization.

The Table 2 protocol has a selection bias: reasoning quality is evaluated only on 100 samples where all models produce correct detections, which systematically excludes hard cases where grounding matters most; this biases the comparison in favor of the proposed method and limits external validity of the judge-score conclusions.

Baseline fairness is uncertain: SIDA baselines are run at their original 336×336 resolution while the benchmark is preprocessed at 1024×1024, and all specialized baselines are retrained by the authors without reporting tuning effort comparable to the proposed model. The large gaps could partly reflect adaptation artifacts rather than architectural advantages.

Novelty positioning is somewhat overstated ('first large-scale medical forgery benchmark' despite MedForensics and related work; pre-hoc reasoning already explored in general AIGC detection). The methodological novelty (GSPO with a coverage-based grounding reward) is a reasonable but incremental combination of known techniques.

Editorial sloppiness undermines confidence: duplicated 'Formatting Reward' bullet in Appendix B.4, typos ('aronud', 'Explainnation', 'Nanao-Banana', 'Mortality-specific' vs 'Modality-specific', 'Forgrey'), inconsistent counts (19 pathologies vs '20 Lesion Types'), the Limitations section says 'two main limitations' then lists three, and footnote 1 has no URL. These suggest the manuscript needed another careful pass.

strengths: MedForge-90K is a substantial and timely resource: ~95K images spanning 3 modalities and 19 pathologies, forged by 10 diverse state-of-the-art text-guided editors applied to authentic scans (a realistic threat model), with ground-truth manipulation boxes derived from Change Vector Analysis and a well-documented Writer-Editor-Diagnoser quality-control loop.

The 'localize-then-analyze' formulation is well-motivated: forcing bbox prediction before reasoning makes explanations inspectable and gives a concrete mechanism (coverage-based reward) for suppressing hallucinated evidence.

The two-stage SFT + forgery-aware GSPO method is clearly specified, including the shaped sigmoid coverage reward and geometric-mean importance ratio, and the ablations (Table 3) cleanly decompose the contribution of grounding vs. format vs. classification rewards.

Evaluation is unusually thorough: in-domain, cross-model, and cross-forgery splits; four external OOD medical deepfake datasets; scalability across four MLLM backbones; IoU diagnostics; a failure-mode analysis; and a (small) human evaluation in addition to MLLM-as-judge.

The paper is honest about unfavorable results: the human evaluation ranks the proposed model 3rd behind Qwen3-VL-Plus, and the discussion of the accuracy-vs-Judge-Score trade-off and the one-sided coverage reward's oversized-box risk is candid.

Reproducibility is well supported: prompts, judge protocol, hyperparameters, model inventory, and split ratios are all documented; code, data, and checkpoints are stated to be released. Limitations (modality coverage, English-only, dual-use risk) are properly discussed.
weaknesses: The 'expert-aligned' supervision is ultimately produced by Gemini 2.5 Pro following expert-written guidelines; the paper never quantitatively validates the generated rationales against independent clinician judgment on a sample (the human eval is 2 trained annotators, not medical experts, on 100 cases). The central claim that rationales are 'medically coherent' is therefore only indirectly supported.

Evaluation of reasoning quality relies on MLLM judges (Qwen3-VL-Plus and Gemini 3 Pro) that are themselves baselines, raising self-preference/style-bias concerns; the disagreement between the judge scores (proposed best) and human evaluation (proposed 3rd) is not fully reconciled.

Detection accuracy is near ceiling (99%+) on the benchmark's own test set, limiting discriminative power for future work; the most informative results are the OOD tables, where margins over the strongest baselines are meaningful but the benchmark itself may be too easy.

The grounding reward is one-sided (coverage without area penalty), which the authors themselves acknowledge could admit degenerate large-box solutions; the reward design is sensible but the analysis here is somewhat post-hoc.

Methodological novelty is moderate: the pipeline is a competent domain adaptation of established components (bbox-then-reason SFT, GRPO/GSPO-style RL with grounding and format rewards); the main contribution is the dataset and the empirical findings rather than a new technique.

Minor issues: the '90K' name conflicts with the reported 95,276 images; equation numbering appears off by one (Eq. 1 is referenced but the visible formula is labeled Eq. 2); human evaluation lacks inter-annotator agreement statistics; annotation of real images as 'satisfaction of biological logic' by an MLM could introduce systematic false-positive supervision not analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and under-explored problem (medical image forgery detection with interpretable, clinically grounded reasoning), with a clear 'localize-then-analyze' motivation

MedForge-90K is a substantial resource: ~95K images spanning three modalities, 19 pathologies, 10 diverse editors, with manipulation masks, structured rationales, and a documented generation/refinement pipeline (Appendix C is fairly detailed)

Reasonably comprehensive experimental design: in-domain, cross-model, and cross-forgery splits, external OOD datasets, ablations over reward components and backbones, and an attempted human evaluation to complement MLLM-as-judge

The paper is transparent about some weaknesses (one-sided coverage reward admitting oversized boxes, coarse localization, failure-mode analyses in Appendix B.3/B.4), and hyperparameters/model choices are documented in Appendix D, aiding reproducibility
weaknesses: The 'expert-aligned' claim is overstated: the detection guidelines are formulated with (unnamed) medical experts, but all rationales are generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro conditioned on CVA-derived boxes fed into the prompt. This creates circularity — the annotation MLLM is told where the forgery is and asked to rationalize it — so the 'grounded reasoning' supervision may largely reflect a single commercial model's templated rationalization, and annotation quality is never independently verified by humans

Benchmark saturation undermines the resource's value: in-domain accuracy is 99.2–99.8% and even OOD datasets reach ~90%+ with tiny error counts (0.76% error). It is unclear MedForge-90K measures clinically meaningful forensic difficulty versus trivial artifact detection (e.g., sticker lesions); a harder, clinically realistic split or adversarial evaluation is missing

Evaluation of the central 'hallucination-free reasoning' claim is compromised: the MLLM judges include Qwen3-VL-Plus, the same family as the proposed model's backbone, inviting self-preference bias; the human evaluation uses only two (non-physician?) annotators on 100 samples and — crucially — the proposed model ranks only 3rd overall behind Qwen3-VL-Plus, contradicting the headline claim of superior reasoning quality

Localization quality is weak (mean IoU 31.5%, median 25.1%) and reported only after the fact; no comparison against dedicated localization baselines, making it hard to judge whether the GSPO grounding reward meaningfully beats simpler localization training

Methodological novelty is limited: GSPO is applied essentially off-the-shelf with a hand-crafted reward; the formatting reward (keyword presence) is trivially gameable; equations 1–10 largely restate standard RLHF/GRPO machinery

Presentation inconsistencies hurt trust: the benchmark is named 'MedForge-90K' but totals 95,276 images (63,286 fake in the inventory vs. 63,286 stated elsewhere with mismatched real/fake ratios); backbone naming fluctuates (Qwen3-VL-8B vs. InternVL3.5-8B); 'Gemini 3 Pro' baselines with future-dated citations suggest unverifiable references

No variance across seeds/runs for main results, no significance testing despite differences sometimes <0.2% (which the paper itself treats as meaningful), and derived-image release from MIMIC/ODIR raises data-licensing questions that are not addressed

The near-perfect accuracy combined with the acknowledged trade-off (w/o Bbox Grounding has higher accuracy) leaves the practical value of the full pipeline under-justified for the detection task itself; the justification rests entirely on reasoning quality, which the evaluation design does not robustly establish

strengths: Highly relevant and timely problem: medically-targeted forgery of authentic scans via modern text-guided editors is a genuine and underexplored threat, and the paper motivates it well.

Substantial resource contribution: MedForge-90K (~95K images, 19 pathologies, 10 modern editors, implant/removal) is constructed with a carefully documented pipeline (writer–editor–diagnoser loop, CVA-derived manipulation masks, structured hierarchical guidelines, full prompt templates in the appendix), which supports reproducibility.

Reasonable and well-motivated method: the localize-then-analyze formulation, structured CoT output, and Forgery-aware GSPO with a coverage-based grounding reward directly target the stated goal of pre-hoc, visually verifiable rationales.

Unusually comprehensive experiments for this area: in-domain, cross-model, cross-forgery settings; OOD evaluation on four unseen datasets; ablations over components, reward terms, and backbones; IoU diagnostics with an explicit reward-hacking analysis; failure-mode breakdowns; and both MLLM-as-judge and human evaluation.

Notable honesty in places: the ablation acknowledges small accuracy costs of interpretability, the human evaluation reports the proposed model ranking 3rd, and the IoU section candidly discusses coarse localization and the risk of oversized-box solutions.
Training details (LoRA config, batch sizes, hyperparameters, GPU setup) and promised release of data, code, and checkpoints support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The 'expert-aligned reasoning supervision' claim is weaker than advertised: rationales are generated by Gemini 2.5/3 Pro using expert-formulated guidelines, but there is no physician validation of the guidelines, no inter-annotator study, and no clinical audit of the resulting annotations. The paper effectively trains and evaluates against LLM-generated rationales, which conflates 'expert-aligned' with 'prompt-conditioned LLM output'.

Benchmark circularity and near-ceiling results: forgeries are generated from known image pairs, manipulation masks are derived from pixel differences between real and forged versions, and the test set shares the construction pipeline. In-domain accuracy is ~99% for the proposed model and even simple ablations exceed 99%, suggesting limited discriminative power; the realistic deployment gap (no ground-truth pair available, unseen editors/attack methods) is only partially probed via the OOD section.

Inconsistent and selectively framed evaluation claims: under the Gemini 3 Pro judge the proposed model (73.9) scores below generic Gemini 3 Pro (76.2), and human evaluation places it below Qwen3-VL-Plus (72.7 vs 76.3), yet the text emphasizes '16.2%/31.2%' improvements against specialized detectors and the strongest VH reduction. The GSPO gain on judge scores is only ~2.5 points, considerably less impressive than headline phrasing suggests.

Mean localization IoU of ~31.6% (median 25%) is coarse, which undercuts the 'visually verifiable, pixel-grounded' framing for a substantial fraction of cases; the coverage-only reward is a plausible contributor and the paper only speculates about future fixes.

The novelty of the methodological component is incremental: GSPO is adapted from prior work, and the main technical addition is the reward composition; the primary contribution is the dataset, so the strength of the paper rests heavily on annotation quality, which is not independently verified.

Minor presentation/consistency issues: 'MedForge-90K' actually contains 95,276 images per Table 10; the 'first large-scale medical forgery benchmark' claim ignores closely related concurrent resources (e.g., Med-Banana-50K, cited); duplicate 'Formatting Reward' bullets in D.4 with conflicting descriptions; base resolution discrepancy (336×336 for baselines vs 1024×1024 preprocessing) may disadvantage some baselines.

MLLM-as-judge for the primary reasoning metric introduces self-preference and model-family bias risks; judges are also the annotation generator (Gemini), and judge behavior is only partially disentangled by the (small, 2-annotator, 100-sample) human study.
